deep.reconstruction:
Title: 'Taylor's theorem following Cauchy's treatment.' The page sets up Cauchy's 1831 (Turin memoir) proof of the power-series expansion of a function of a complex variable through circular means.

(1) Hypothesis. Z = f(z) with z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) = r e^{iθ}. Z and dZ/dz vary continuously ('nach der Stetigkeit fortschreitet') for all r between R^0 and R', i.e. on a closed annulus. Implicitly Z is single-valued, so Z is 2π-periodic in θ.

(2) Definition. Put S(r) = (1/2π) ∫_0^{2π} Z(r e^{iθ}) dθ, the mean of Z over the circle |z| = r, with r held constant. Claim: S is constant for R^0 ≤ r ≤ R'.

Proof as written:
- Differentiate under the integral sign: 2π dS/dr = ∫_0^{2π} ∂Z/∂r dθ = ∫_0^{2π} Z'(z) (∂z/∂r) dθ.
- From log z = log r + iθ one gets dz/z = dr/r + i dθ. Hence ∂z/∂r = z/r and ∂z/∂θ = iz.
- So ∂z/∂r is a multiple of ∂z/∂θ. Gauss writes ∂z/∂r = (i/r) ∂z/∂θ; the correct factor is 1/(ir) = -i/r.
- With ∂Z/∂θ = Z'(z) ∂z/∂θ this gives 2π dS/dr = (const/r) ∫_0^{2π} ∂Z/∂θ dθ.
- [My completion] This equals (const/r)[Z(r e^{2πi}) − Z(r)] = 0 by single-valuedness.
- Hence S is independent of r, 'as far as the basic principles (Grund-principien) of the differential calculus are valid'. The next page confirms this applies on all of [R^0, R'].

Continuation on the next page (context only):
- (3) If R^0 = 0 can be taken, S is constant down to r = 0, so S = Z(0). This is the mean-value property f(0) = (1/2π)∫ f(re^{iθ}) dθ.
- (4) Apply this to Ω = x(X − A)/(x − a), with X = f(x) and A = f(a). Ω vanishes at x = 0, so ∫_0^{2π} Ω dθ = 0.
- [My completion of where this leads] Since ∫ x/(x−a) dθ = 2π for |a| < r, this gives A = (1/2π)∫_0^{2π} xX/(x−a) dθ. This is Cauchy's integral formula in mean-value form.
- Expanding x/(x−a) = Σ (a/x)^n then yields the Taylor series of f(a) with coefficients (1/2π)∫ X x^{−n} dθ. This is Cauchy's 1831 proof of Taylor's theorem and of the convergence of the series up to the nearest singularity.
errors: Sign slip: from dz/dθ = iz and dz/dr = z/r it follows that dz/dr = (1/(ir)) dz/dθ = -(i/r) dz/dθ, not (i/r) dz/dθ as written. The same wrong sign appears in 2π dS/dr = ∫ (i/r) dZ/dθ dθ. It is harmless because the integral is 0.
The final step ∫_0^{2π} ∂Z/∂θ dθ = 0 is not justified on the page. It needs Z to be single-valued (2π-periodic in θ) on each circle. This is implicit in the hypothesis but not stated.
Notational inconsistency: the bounds are written R^0 and R' in §1 but R and R' in §2.
Differentiation under the integral sign is used without comment. The hypotheses (continuity of Z and dZ/dz on the closed annulus) do suffice for it.

results.what: The circular mean S(r) = (1/2π)∫_0^{2π} f(re^{iθ}) dθ of a function with continuous complex derivative on an annulus is independent of r. Proof: dS/dr = (1/(2πir))∫ ∂f/∂θ dθ = 0.
results.modern_name: Cauchy's integral theorem for an annulus / mean-value property (proof by differentiating the circular mean with respect to the radius)
results.usually_credited_to: A.-L. Cauchy, Turin memoir of 1831 (Mémoire sur la mécanique céleste / 'Résumé d'un mémoire...'), building on his integral theorem of 1825

results.what: Setup (continued on the next page) of the Taylor expansion via A = (1/2π)∫ xX/(x−a) dθ, obtained from the vanishing mean of x(X−A)/(x−a).
results.modern_name: Cauchy integral formula and Cauchy–Taylor theorem (convergence of the power series inside the disc of holomorphy)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is explicitly titled as an exposition of Taylor's theorem 'nach Cauchys Behandlung'. It reproduces Cauchy's 1831 circular-mean proof faithfully, with a harmless sign slip. Gauss's own priority on the integral theorem (letter to Bessel, 1811) is already well known. A study note on Cauchy's published method adds nothing unexpected.

checkable.asserts: Gauss's written relation dz/dr = (i/r) dz/dθ is off by sign: result is 2*exp(I*t), not 0
The mean of exp(z) over |z| = r equals exp(0) = 1, independent of r (may need series/simplify)
The circular mean of a polynomial is its constant term: 2*pi*1

transcription_corrections: Last line: 'so weit die Grenz[?]' should read 'so weit die Grund' (continuing as 'Grund-principien der Differentialrechnung' on the next page).
In §2 the bounds are written 'R und R'' (no superscript 0), as transcribed. This is consistent with the image but inconsistent with 'R^0' in §1.
The struck-out word before 'innerhalb' is illegible in the image; '[-die-]' is a guess.
